external_dependencies: The public key infrastructure that issues the DoD-approved certificates, and the certificate authority trust chain each receiver and sender validates against, are managed outside the application.
Forwarder-side settings in outputs.conf live on a separate host by definition, so on an indexer only the receiving half of this criterion can be read.

Whether the address or name that connection_host records is the true origin depends on the network path: an intervening relay, proxy or load balancer substitutes its own address, and DNS must resolve consistently for the "dns" setting to be meaningful.
Mapping an authenticated source to an organization, system, application or individual is an organizational naming and attribution scheme; the application records the identifier it is given.
finding_statement: Splunk does not uniquely identify and authenticate the source of transferred data: connection_host is set to "none" on a receiving input, the receiver's TLS certificate or client-certificate requirement is unset in inputs.conf [SSL], the forwarder presents no client certificate or does not verify the receiver, Splunk Web is not served over HTTPS, or a UDP input is configured, which the product STIG prohibits because it cannot authenticate a sender.

application_contribution: Splunk's own role-based access control is where the separation is expressed: capabilities are disabled by default and each authorize.conf [role_<roleName>] stanza grants them explicitly, so the product can hold a distinct administrative role whose security-relevant capabilities no non-privileged role inherits.
citation: importRoles present and grantableRoles present test nothing about separation and fail compliant roles. A role is defined by its capability lines - "<capability> = <enabled>", and "'enabled' is the only accepted value here, as capabilities are disabled by default" - while importRoles defaults to "A role imports no other roles" (authorize.conf.spec:67-84), so a non-privileged role that imports nothing is exactly what this requirement wants and a present test reports it as a finding. grantableRoles is narrower still: it bounds what a user holding "edit_roles_grantable" and "edit_user" may manage (authorize.conf.spec:86-98), so requiring it of every role stanza is a finding against every role that delegates no user management, which is most of them. Neither key says whether a non-privileged account can reach security-relevant information or functions; that is decided by the capability set of each role and by the organization's designation of which roles and accounts are privileged, neither of which this vocabulary can express over a generic [role_<roleName>] stanza. The SRG's subject is also "non-privileged accounts on the hosting system", which is the operating system's account base, so the larger part of this objective was never the application's to carry.
external_dependencies: The SRG scopes this to non-privileged accounts on the hosting system: operating system accounts, their group membership, and their access to the installation directory and configuration files are carried by the operating system.
Which Splunk roles and accounts count as privileged is an organizational determination the application cannot infer from any value.
Where authentication is delegated, the directory service or identity provider decides group membership and therefore which role a user receives.
An assessor reviews the capability grants in each authorize.conf [role_<roleName>] stanza against the organization's list of administrative and non-privileged roles.
finding_statement: Non-privileged Splunk roles hold capabilities that reach security-relevant information or functions, instead of those capabilities being confined to a distinct administrative role in authorize.conf.
manual_reason: Separation depends on which capabilities each role carries and which accounts hold which role, and the vocabulary cannot name "the non-privileged roles" without the organization's own role assignment; the SRG's subject is also accounts on the hosting system.

application_contribution: For accounts held in Splunk's own authentication system, Splunk enforces the lockout itself: authentication.conf [splunk_auth] lockoutUsers turns lockout on, lockoutAttempts sets how many unsuccessful logins may occur before the account is locked, lockoutThresholdMins sets how long the failed-attempt counter runs before resetting, and lockoutMins sets how long the lockout is held.
citation: SRG-APP-000345-AU-000400 check text ('lock out the account until released by an administrator when 3 consecutive invalid attempts during a 15 minute period is exceeded'); product STIG SPLK-CL-000070 fix ('Modify the following lines in the authentication.conf file under the [splunk_auth]: lockoutUsers = True or 1') and check ('If the lockoutUsers is missing or is configured to 0 or False, this is a finding'); authentication.conf.spec:437 ([splunk_auth]), authentication.conf.spec:514-519 (lockoutUsers = <boolean>, default true), authentication.conf.spec:532-541 (lockoutAttempts = <positive integer>, unsuccessful attempts before lockout, must occur within lockoutThresholdMins, minimum 1, maximum 64, default 5), authentication.conf.spec:543-552 (lockoutThresholdMins = <positive integer>, minutes that must pass from the first failed login before the counter resets, minimum 1, maximum 120, default 5), authentication.conf.spec:521-530 (lockoutMins = <positive integer>, minutes a user is locked out, minimum 1, maximum 1440, default 30)

conditions.rationale: The product STIG fix for SPLK-CL-000070 sets lockoutUsers to True or 1 and its check makes a missing value or 0 or False a finding; authentication.conf.spec:514-515 declares the setting as a boolean in [splunk_auth].

The check text locks the account when 3 consecutive invalid attempts is exceeded. authentication.conf.spec:532-535 defines lockoutAttempts as the number of unsuccessful login attempts that can occur before a user is locked out, with a default of 5; a value of 3 or lower locks on the attempt after the third failure.
authentication.conf.spec:537-538 states any value less than 1 is ignored and the minimum value is 1, so a value below 1 silently reverts and enforces nothing.

The check text requires the three attempts be counted across a 15 minute period. authentication.conf.spec:543-546 defines lockoutThresholdMins as the minutes that must pass from the first failed login before the counter resets, with a default of 5; a window shorter than 15 lets the counter reset inside the period the requirement measures.
authentication.conf.spec:549 states the maximum accepted value is 120, so any larger value is outside the setting's permitted range.

external_dependencies: Splunk's native lockout always expires on its own - authentication.conf.spec:526-528 caps lockoutMins at 1440 minutes - so the product cannot hold an account locked until an administrator releases it. The administrator-release portion of AC-7 b is carried by an organizational procedure in which an administrator unlocks the account through Splunk user management, and by the organization accepting the automatic expiry of the configured lockout period.

[splunk_auth] governs only accounts held in Splunk's native authentication system. Where authType is LDAP, SAML or ProxySSO, the failed-attempt counting and lockout are enforced by the directory service or identity provider and are assessed against that component.

authentication.conf.spec:517-519, 528-530, 539-541 and 550-552 state that on search head cluster members the lockout state applies per member rather than to the whole cluster, so cluster-wide enforcement depends on the deployment topology.

Holding a locked account until an administrator releases it, which authentication.conf does not express: lockoutMins sets a duration whose documented maximum is 1440 minutes, and no value means release by an administrator only.
finding_statement: Splunk Enterprise does not lock native accounts on three failed logins in 15 minutes: authentication.conf [splunk_auth] lockoutUsers is missing or set to 0 or False, lockoutAttempts is absent or greater than 3, lockoutThresholdMins is absent or less than 15 so the failed-attempt counter resets inside the measured period, or lockoutMins is not explicitly configured.

application_contribution: Splunk has no account expiration date for its native accounts - the one expiry mechanism it ships governs passwords, not accounts - so the application's contribution is limited to honoring, at the next authentication, the decision of whatever authority holds the account lifecycle.
citation: All three conditions are invention, and two of them are also vacuous. web-features.conf [feature:identity_sidecar_scim] enabled controls only "whether or not Splunk Web displays Automated User Management (AUM) controls for System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM) in the SAML configuration dialog page" and defaults to true (web-features.conf.spec:400-410): it is a dialog visibility toggle that provisions nothing and cannot bear on account expiry at all. server.conf [teleport_supervisor] disabled launches the process that "handles authorization tokens for System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM) operations" and already defaults to false, meaning launched (server.conf.spec:6584-6591), so the condition is unfounded in any source text - this SRG carries no product STIG rule, so both check and fix text are the SRG's own abstract wording - and cannot fail a default installation. authType not_equals Splunk forces delegated authentication the check text never asks for, the same over-reach as in SRG-APP-000315-WSR-000003, and fails an instance whose account lifecycle is managed by an organizational procedure instead. The nearest native setting is expireUserAccounts, and the specification is explicit that it "Specifies whether password expiration is enabled", sitting beside expirePasswordDays and expireAlertDays (authentication.conf.spec:487-507): that is password expiry under the identification and authentication controls, not the account expiration date this requirement's CCI-003627 asks about. The two keys the inventory carries for this requirement as undeclared, scimSupportedDomains and scsSyncUserDeletes, appear in no .conf.spec in the 10.4.2 set, so no criterion can be written over them.
external_dependencies: The enterprise directory service or identity provider holds the account expiration date and must disable or deprovision the account on expiry; Splunk honors that decision only at the next authentication.

Where accounts are provisioned through SCIM, the provisioning authority sends the disable or delete; the receiving path exists in the product but the decision and the transmission are the authority's.
The organization's account review and offboarding procedure determines when an account has expired.
An assessor confirms the account lifecycle authority and its expiry handling, because the application exposes no expiration value to read.
finding_statement: No application-layer finding is available: Splunk native accounts have no expiration date field, so the assessor records the authority that holds the account lifecycle and verifies expiry handling there; raise a finding only where no authority outside the application disables expired accounts.
manual_reason: Splunk native accounts carry no expiration date field, and nothing in the 10.4.2 specification set expresses one, so no configuration value can decide whether expired accounts are disabled.

application_contribution: Splunk cannot itself determine that an account no longer belongs to a user; it keeps the path open on which an external identity authority's disable or delete arrives, and surfaces the trace a departed owner leaves behind in scheduled searches.
citation: limits.conf [system_checks] orphan_searches "Enables/disables automatic UI message notifications to admins for scheduled saved searches with invalid owners" and defaults to enabled (limits.conf.spec:4486-4498). It raises a message about a search; it disables no account, so equals:enabled yields a confident status for a requirement it does not touch, and because enabled is already the default the condition can only fail an instance that has turned the notification off - a finding over a UI message, not over account disabling. The server.conf [teleport_supervisor] disabled and web-features.conf [feature:identity_sidecar_scim] enabled conditions are the SCIM token process and the SAML dialog toggle described under SRG-APP-000700-WSR-000100: both already sit in the state the criterion demands by default (server.conf.spec:6584-6591, web-features.conf.spec:400-410), neither disables an account, and neither appears in any check or fix text, since this SRG carries no product STIG rule. The inventory's scimSupportedDomains and scsSyncUserDeletes keys exist in no .conf.spec in the 10.4.2 set. Nothing in the product expresses disassociation, so this is case 4: manual, with the lifecycle authority named in the external dependencies rather than asserted through a proxy setting.
external_dependencies: The enterprise directory service or identity provider determines when an account is no longer associated to a user and must push the resulting disable or delete; Splunk honors it at the next authentication.
Where accounts are provisioned through SCIM, the provisioning authority issues the deprovisioning call.
The organization's offboarding procedure, and the review that finds accounts with no owner, are procedural and outside the application.
An assessor may use Splunk's orphaned scheduled search notification as evidence that departed owners are detected, but it notifies rather than disables.
finding_statement: No application-layer finding is available: Splunk has no setting that detects an account with no associated user or disables it, so the assessor records the identity authority that performs the disable; raise a finding only where no authority outside the application does so.
manual_reason: No setting in the 10.4.2 specification set determines that an account is no longer associated to a user, or disables it on that basis, so configuration cannot decide this requirement.

application_contribution: Splunk cannot itself determine that an account no longer belongs to a user, so its contribution is to honor the disable or delete issued by whatever authority holds the account lifecycle at the next authentication.
citation: The three conditions repeat the defects corrected in SRG-APP-000700-WSR-000100 and SRG-APP-000705-AU-000110. authType not_equals Splunk forces delegated authentication the check text does not ask for and fails an instance whose account lifecycle is managed procedurally, which is over-reach against the documented default of Splunk (authentication.conf.spec:30-33). server.conf [teleport_supervisor] disabled already defaults to false, launched, and governs SCIM authorization token handling rather than account state (server.conf.spec:6584-6591). web-features.conf [feature:identity_sidecar_scim] enabled defaults to true and only decides whether Splunk Web shows Automated User Management controls in the SAML configuration dialog (web-features.conf.spec:400-410); a dialog toggle cannot disable an account. This SRG carries no product STIG rule, so neither value has any source text behind it. The inventory for this requirement is also unusable: the keys it lists under server.conf [teleport_supervisor] - Splunk, Web, scimSupportedDomains and scsSyncUserDeletes - are not settings of that stanza, which defines only disabled, and none of the last two appear in any .conf.spec in the 10.4.2 set, so no criterion can be written over them.
external_dependencies: The enterprise directory service or identity provider determines when an account is no longer associated to a user and must push the disable or delete.
Where accounts are provisioned through SCIM, the provisioning authority issues the deprovisioning call; the product carries the receiving path only.
The organization's offboarding and periodic account review procedures are outside the application.
An assessor confirms the lifecycle authority and its disassociation handling, because the application exposes no value to read.
finding_statement: No application-layer finding is available: Splunk has no setting that detects an account with no associated user or disables it, so the assessor records the identity authority that performs the disable; raise a finding only where no authority outside the application does so.
manual_reason: The product exposes no value that determines whether an account is still associated to a user or disables it on that basis; the account lifecycle authority is confirmed by the assessor.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise can encrypt both of its own administrative entry points - Splunk Web through web.conf [settings] enableSplunkWebSSL and the splunkd management and KV Store ports through server.conf [sslConfig] enableSplunkdSSL - which is the logical separation by encryption that the requirement's own discussion names as the method; it can additionally narrow admission to each of those listeners with acceptFrom, but the set of networks that constitutes the maintenance path is an organization-defined list and is not derivable from Splunk configuration.
citation:
CHANGED. Three corrections to the criterion as derived; the two TLS conditions are kept, and both acceptFrom conditions are removed from the pass criterion.

1. OVER-REACH - "web.conf [settings] acceptFrom present" removed. The SRG check text (inventory/groups/MA.json, SRG-APP-000880-WSR-000290) asks only that the maintenance session be separated from other network sessions by logically separated communications paths, and the discussion names exactly one mechanism: "Communications paths can be logically separated using encryption." Nothing in the check or fix text mentions source-network admission. There is no product STIG rule for this requirement (stig_reference is empty and the group's own determination records stig_reference_status "no_reference"), so no product authority supplies an acceptFrom value either. An instance that carries TLS on Splunk Web and on the splunkd management port has done what the discussion names; failing it because acceptFrom sits at its default converts the organization's decision to separate the path at the network layer - the dependency this same criterion already records externally - into an application finding. That is case 3: the application's share is tested, the remainder is recorded, and no finding is raised against Splunk.

2. DIRECTION / ineffective test - "web.conf [settings] acceptFrom not_equals *" removed. Even if admission control were in scope here, a plain string inequality cannot decide whether the list is open. web.conf.spec:1080-1096 defines acceptFrom as an ordered rule list ("Separate multiple rules with commas or spaces ... The input applies rules in order, and uses the first one that matches") in which a bare "*" is only one of four rule formats, and the specification's own worked example at web.conf.spec:1093-1095 is "!10.1/16, *", described as allowing "connections from everywhere except the 10.1.*.* network." That value is as permissive as the "*" default for every network but one, and it satisfies not_equals:*. The condition therefore returns a confident PASS for precisely the configurations it exists to fail, which is worse than having no condition. Writing it instead as a matches regex that rejects any unprefixed "*" term would make it evaluable, but it would still be the over-reach of item 1, so it is removed rather than repaired.

3. source_of_value corrected from srg_check_text to spec_default. The check text for this requirement is tautological - it restates the title and names no setting, value, or threshold - so it cannot be the source of "true" or "false". The direction of each surviving condition is fixed by the vendor-documented default: web.conf.spec:73 "Default: false" makes enableSplunkWebSSL an affirmative requirement, and server.conf.spec:733 "Default: true" makes enableSplunkdSSL a prohibition on disabling. Attributing those operands to the check text invites an assessor to look for them there, find nothing, and reject the row.

NOT CHANGED, and deliberately so: the conf and stanza on enableSplunkdSSL. The derived criterion placed it at server.conf [sslConfig], which is correct per server.conf.spec:712 and :724 and matches the group's own recorded mechanism. The defect is in the inventory, not the criterion - assess/inventory/checks.tsv line 1180 assigns enableSplunkdSSL to web.conf [settings] and flags it key_status "undeclared", which is accurate in that web.conf has no such key: the only web.conf.spec occurrences of the string are cross-references at :156 and :1626-equivalent prose. A condition bound to that TSV row could never resolve against a merged configuration. The row should be repointed to server.conf [sslConfig]; conditions must not be attached to it as written.

ALSO CONSIDERED AND EXCLUDED, because checks.tsv declares them for this requirement and a reader will ask why they are absent from conditions. requireClientCert (web.conf.spec:151) is mutual authentication, not path separation; mandating it here would exceed the discussion's stated method, and web.conf.spec:95-97 requires it to be "false" when an encrypted private key is used, so a blanket demand would contradict a supported TLS configuration. mgmtHostPort (web.conf.spec:35-43) is "The IP address and host port where Splunk Web looks for the splunkd process" - a client-side address with a documented default of 0.0.0.0:8089 - so it does not restrict what the management listener admits and a condition over it would test nothing about separation. httpport (web.conf.spec:28) selects a listening port, and port number alone carries no separation. listenOnIPv6 selects an address family. server.conf [httpServerListener:<ip>:<port>] ssl (server.conf.spec:1612-1629) does bind an additional REST listener to one interface, but server.conf.spec:1620-1623 states these stanzas "need not be present" on a normal instance and ssl defaults to "true", so a condition over an optional stanza that usually does not exist would be unsatisfiable on a correctly configured instance.

conditions.rationale: The discussion states "Communications paths can be logically separated using encryption," naming encryption as the mechanism; Splunk Web is one of the application's two administrative entry points, and web.conf.spec:70-73 documents enableSplunkWebSSL as "Toggle between http or https ... Set to true to enable https and SSL" with "Default: false", so an unset key leaves the administrative interface in cleartext and the test must demand the explicit "true".

Same discussion sentence, applied to the second administrative entry point. server.conf.spec:724-733, in the [sslConfig] stanza declared at server.conf.spec:712, documents enableSplunkdSSL as governing "TLS/SSL on the management port (default 8089) and app key value store (KV Store, default 8191) network ports," with "A value of 'false' means that splunkd does not run TLS on any port" and "Default: true". Because the product default is already secure, not_equals:false is the correct direction: it passes an absent key running the documented default and raises a finding only on an explicit disable, where equals:true would produce a false finding against an instance running the secure default. The documented vocabulary for this <boolean> is literally "true" and "false" (server.conf.spec:728-730), so the operand stays inside the specification and is not broadened to spellings the spec set does not document for a <boolean>.

external_dependencies: Whether the resulting management path is in fact separated from search and data-ingestion sessions - a management VLAN or out-of-band network, a VPN concentrator, a jump host, or a reverse proxy fronting Splunk Web - is carried by the network baseline and evidenced in the system's network documentation; no Splunk setting can report it.

Selection of the networks that constitute the maintenance path is an organization-defined list recorded in the system security plan and the remote access policy. Where the organization elects to enforce that list inside the application, web.conf [settings] acceptFrom (web.conf.spec:1080) and server.conf [httpServer] acceptFrom (server.conf.spec:1345) express it, but the list itself originates outside the application and is not decidable from Splunk configuration.

The physically separated branch of MA-4 (4) (b) (2), where the organization elects physical rather than logical separation, is furnished entirely by the network baseline; the application carries only the logical, encryption-based branch.
finding_statement: Splunk Enterprise does not encrypt both of its administrative entry points - web.conf [settings] enableSplunkWebSSL does not have the value "true", or server.conf [sslConfig] enableSplunkdSSL is set to "false" - so the nonlocal maintenance session is not logically separated from other network sessions by encryption to the extent the application is able to do so.

application_contribution: Splunk verifies on every startup, and on a recurring interval thereafter, that the files installed with the running version still match the release manifest, and reports any file that was removed or altered.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000131-WSR-000051 check text; limits.conf.spec:4450 (installed_files_integrity = enabled | log_only | disabled, default enabled), limits.conf.spec:4468 (installed_files_integrity_interval, default 12h), limits.conf.spec:4475

conditions.rationale: The check text asks whether the server "validates files before the files are implemented into the running configuration"; of the three permitted values, only "enabled" both posts the detected problem to the bulletin board and writes it to the daemon log, while "log_only" suppresses the notice and "disabled" attempts no check at all.

The check text treats validation as a condition of the running configuration rather than a one-time act at install, so the recurring interval must be expressed; the setting has no effect when the integrity check itself is disabled.

external_dependencies: Verification of installation media and app packages before they reach the installation directory, carried by the operating system package manager's signature checking and by the organization's software acceptance procedure.

app.conf [install] install_source_checksum records the checksum of the package a given app was installed from, but the platform populates it automatically and the specification directs that it not be set by hand, so it is evidence rather than a control the assessor can require (app.conf.spec:158).
indexes.conf enableDataIntegrityControl hashes indexed data, not the product's own installed files, so it does not bear on this objective (indexes.conf.spec:594).
finding_statement: Splunk's installed-file integrity verification is not enabled, so the application does not verify that the files of the running installation still match the release manifest.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise 10.4.2 exposes no configuration setting that requires a digital signature, a review record, or a test record on an app or expansion module before it is loaded, so the application cannot decide this requirement; the nearest controls it does hold - confining who may install apps and keeping the instance from reaching the remote app repository - are assessed under SRG-APP-000810-AU-000250.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000131-WSR-000073 check and fix text; absence of any governing setting across the 10.4.2 specification set (app.conf.spec, authorize.conf.spec, limits.conf.spec)
external_dependencies: Signing of app and module packages and verification of that signature before installation, carried by the package producer and by the organization's app review and approval procedure.
Separation of development and test work from the production instance, carried by the deployment design rather than by any setting on the instance.
Ownership and modes on the app directories, which keep an unreviewed module from being placed there, carried by the operating system.
finding_statement: Not a finding against the application: Splunk exposes no setting bearing on module review, testing, or signing. Record the organization's app review and package signing procedure as the responsible control, and note that the application cannot enforce it.
manual_reason: No .conf setting in the 10.4.2 specification set governs the review, test, or signature state of an app or expansion module, and the check inventory attaches no conf/stanza/key to this requirement. There is nothing in the application's configuration for a condition to read.

application_contribution: Splunk can turn each role-bearing service on an instance on or off independently - Splunk Web, the KV Store, and distributed search - so that an instance carries only the roles its deployment design calls for.
citation: SPLK-CL-000300 check and fix text; web.conf.spec:23 (startwebserver = [0 | 1], default 1), server.conf.spec:5234 (kvstore disabled, default false), distsearch.conf.spec:36 (distributedSearch disabled, default false)

conditions.rationale: The product STIG fix text requires that, where the installation is distributed, "each instance only with the server roles necessary for the desired functions" be set. Which value is correct depends on the role the design assigns, so the application's share is that the switch is declared rather than inherited from the shipped default of 1.

The KV Store is a separate process that a search-head role needs and an indexer-only role does not; the product STIG fix text asks that unused roles not be configured, so this switch must be declared for the instance's role rather than left at the default of false.

Distributed search is on by default, so an instance that is not a search head carries the capability unless the setting is declared; the product STIG check calls a configured but unused role a finding.

external_dependencies: Which roles a given instance is meant to carry, which comes from the distributed deployment design and the system security plan; the product STIG check reads the Monitoring Console mode and the role assignment, and marks a standalone installation not applicable because every function it provides is then necessary.

Non-essential capabilities of the host outside the application - operating system services, packages, and browser plug-ins on analyst workstations - carried by the operating system and the workstation build.
finding_statement: The role-bearing services the application can switch off - Splunk Web, the KV Store, and distributed search - are left at their shipped defaults rather than declared for this instance's role, so the configuration does not show that only the necessary capabilities are enabled.

application_contribution: Splunk can hand authentication and account management to an external directory service or identity provider through authentication.conf, so that the application is not the place where accounts for its users are created and maintained.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000015 discussion and check text; authentication.conf.spec:30 (authType = [Splunk|LDAP|Scripted|SAML|ProxySSO], default Splunk), authentication.conf.spec:44 (authSettings)

conditions.rationale: The discussion states that "user management for the hosted applications should be done through a facility that is built for enterprise-wide user management, like LDAP and Active Directory." Of the five permitted values the specification lists, only "Splunk" makes the application its own account authority; the other four delegate it.

The specification defines authSettings as the key that names the stanza holding the chosen authentication system's configuration, so an external authType with no strategy named does not actually delegate anything.

external_dependencies: The directory service or identity provider itself, and the account lifecycle it runs - password complexity, lockout after failed logins, and management of temporary and emergency accounts - carried by that service.
Splunk retains a small native account store for break-glass access regardless of authType; whether those accounts are limited to that purpose is an organizational access-approval matter.
finding_statement: Splunk is configured for native authentication, or names no external strategy, so the application is performing user management for its own hosted views rather than deferring it to the enterprise directory service.

application_contribution: Splunk can deactivate each service and function it ships - Splunk Web, the KV Store, distributed search - and can set every installed app to a declared enabled or disabled state, which is the product's equivalent of deactivating a feature.
citation: SPLK-CL-000300 fix text; app.conf.spec:124 (state = disabled | enabled, default enabled), web.conf.spec:23, server.conf.spec:5234, distsearch.conf.spec:36

conditions.rationale: The fix text directs that features and processes not needed for operation be deactivated. In Splunk, a feature is delivered as an app, and the specification states that a disabled app's configurations are ignored, so each app's state must be declared rather than inherited from the default of enabled.
Splunk Web is a service the product can be run without; it starts by default, so an instance that does not need it must declare the setting.
The KV Store is a separate process the instance can run without, and it is enabled by default, so a role that does not use it must declare the setting.
Distributed search is enabled by default, so an instance that does not fan out searches carries the function unless the setting is declared.

external_dependencies: Which features and processes the deployment actually needs, which comes from the deployment design; the product STIG marks a standalone installation not applicable because all functions it provides are then necessary.
Services and packages installed on the host outside the application, carried by the operating system build.
finding_statement: The services and apps the application can deactivate are left at their shipped defaults rather than declared, so the configuration does not show that only the services and functions needed for operation are running.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise ships no forward- or reverse-proxy service for third-party traffic, so there is no proxy function to uninstall; the one relay it does offer is the app-browse channel to the remote applications repository, and the application can close it.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000076 check and fix text; server.conf.spec:1734 (allowInternetAccess), server.conf.spec:1201 ([proxyConfig] is an outbound client setting), web.conf.spec:1016 (tools.proxy.on describes being behind a reverse proxy, default false)

conditions.rationale: The fix text directs that any service or module used by the server to act as a proxy be removed. This setting is what lets the instance relay a browser's app-browse requests outward to the remote applications repository on the user's behalf, and it is the only relay of third-party traffic the product offers; the specification defines it as a boolean, so either spelling of false closes it.

external_dependencies: Any reverse proxy, load balancer, or egress proxy placed in front of or beside the instance, carried by that network component rather than by the application; web.conf tools.proxy.on only tells Splunk that such a proxy is present so it can read the forwarded headers, and server.conf [proxyConfig] only tells splunkd to send its own outbound requests through one - neither makes Splunk a proxy for other hosts (web.conf.spec:1016, server.conf.spec:1201).

web.conf enable_proxy_write governs the /splunkd endpoint that Splunk Web's own interface uses to reach the daemon; it is internal to the product's user interface, not a proxy for third-party traffic, and setting it false breaks the interface and the client SDKs (web.conf.spec:371).
finding_statement: The instance is permitted to reach the remote applications repository, so the application still relays user-initiated requests to an outside service on the user's behalf.

application_contribution: Splunk delivers its tutorial content, sample dashboards, and example apps as apps, each of which the application can set to a disabled state and hide from the app menu, which is the strongest removal the running configuration can express.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000077 check and fix text; app.conf.spec:124 (state), app.conf.spec:287 (is_visible)

conditions.rationale: The fix text directs that documentation, sample code, example applications, and tutorials be removed. Within the configuration the equivalent is an explicit state for each installed app, since the specification states that a disabled app's configurations are ignored and the default is enabled.
The check asks whether such content is reachable; is_visible controls whether an app appears in the Splunk Web app menu, so it must be declared for any app retained on the instance.

external_dependencies: Physical removal of the sample, tutorial, and documentation app directories from the installation, carried by the operating system file system and the installation procedure.

The installer's option set - whether the distributed package offers an exclude choice and an uninstall facility - which is a property of the package, not of the running configuration an assessor reads.
finding_statement: Sample, tutorial, and documentation apps are left without a declared state or visibility, so the application does not show that the example content shipped with the product is disabled and out of reach.

application_contribution: The one account the Splunk installation itself creates is the administrator defined in user-seed.conf at first start; the application can show that no such seeded account definition remains in the configuration.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000078 check and fix text; user-seed.conf.spec:25 ([user_info]), user-seed.conf.spec:28 (USERNAME)

conditions.rationale: The check makes any account not used by an installed feature a finding. user-seed.conf exists only to create the initial administrator at first start, so a USERNAME still declared there is an installation-created account definition left in the configuration after it has served its purpose.

external_dependencies: Enumeration and removal of accounts in Splunk's own user store, which is held in the instance's user data rather than in a .conf file an assessor can read, so it is reviewed through the user administration interface.
Operating system accounts created by the installation package, carried by the operating system.
Account inventory in the directory service where authentication is external, carried by that service.
finding_statement: A seeded installation account definition remains in user-seed.conf, so the application still carries an account created by the installation process rather than by an installed feature in use.

application_contribution: Every utility, plug-in, and module Splunk adds beyond the core daemon arrives as an app or as an optional process, and the application can set each app's state explicitly, record whether the app permits being disabled, and switch off the optional KV Store process.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000080 check and fix text; app.conf.spec:124 (state), app.conf.spec:154 (allows_disable, default true), server.conf.spec:5234 (kvstore disabled)

conditions.rationale: The fix text directs that utility programs, services, and modules not needed for operation be removed. Within the configuration the equivalent is a declared state for each installed app, since the default is enabled and a disabled app's configurations are ignored.

The check asks whether the product provides a facility to customize what is installed. allows_disable is the setting that records whether a given app can be turned off at all, so it must be declared for a retained app to show that the facility exists for it.
The KV Store is an optional process rather than part of the core daemon and runs by default, so an instance that no installed feature requires it on must declare the setting.

external_dependencies: The installer's option set and uninstall facility, which are properties of the distributed package rather than of the running configuration.
Utility programs present on the host outside the application, carried by the operating system build.
Which app-supplied utilities the deployment genuinely needs, carried by the app review procedure.
finding_statement: Installed apps carry no declared state or disable property, or the optional KV Store process is left at its default, so the application does not show that only the utilities and modules needed for operation are present and active.

application_contribution: Splunk's static file handler maps an extension to a MIME type and returns the file; it never hands content to a shell. The places where the product will run an operating system program are the script alert action and scripted search commands and REST handlers, and the application can leave the script action unconfigured and unused.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000081 check and fix text; alert_actions.conf.spec:517 ([script]), alert_actions.conf.spec:518 (filename, default empty string), savedsearches.conf.spec:403 (action.script, default false), server.conf.spec:1656 ([mimetype-extension-map])

conditions.rationale: The check makes it a finding if a user of the server can invoke operating system shell programs. The script alert action runs the named file from the installation's script directory, and on UNIX a plain shell script is accepted with no further requirement, so no filename declared means no shell program is reachable through this path; the specification gives the default as an empty string.

A saved search is how a user triggers the script action. The specification defines action.script as a boolean, default false, so requiring it off keeps a user-triggered search from invoking an operating system program.

external_dependencies: Whether a shell is reachable by the Splunk service account at all, carried by the operating system through the account's shell, the file modes on interpreters, and any mandatory access control policy.

Review of any app-supplied custom search command or scripted REST handler that legitimately invokes an interpreter, carried by the app review procedure; the MIME map itself only names content types for static files and cannot invoke a program (server.conf.spec:1656).
finding_statement: A script is configured for the script alert action, or the script action is enabled on a saved search, so a user of the application can cause an operating system program to run.

application_contribution: A script mapping in Splunk is a custom search command stanza that binds a command name to a file and an interpreter; the application can show that no mapping still names a retired interpreter version.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000082 check and fix text; commands.conf.spec:57 (python.version = {default|python|python2|python3|python3.7|python3.9|latest}), commands.conf.spec:68 (filename), commands.conf.spec:53 (type)

conditions.rationale: The check makes a script mapping that the server or its hosted views do not need a finding, and the fix directs its removal. Of the interpreter versions the specification permits for a command mapping, python2 is the retired one, so a mapping that still selects it is a mapping to a vulnerable script interpreter.

external_dependencies: Which command mappings the deployment's searches and dashboards still use, carried by the app review procedure; the application cannot tell an unused mapping from a rarely used one.
Removal of the script files themselves from the app directories, carried by the operating system file system.
finding_statement: A custom search command mapping still selects the retired python2 interpreter, so the application retains a mapping to a script interpreter that is no longer supported.

application_contribution: Splunk Web serves static content only from a declared directory beneath a declared endpoint, and it can be kept from generating a directory listing, so the files it will return are limited to those the views reference rather than whatever the directory holds.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000083 check and fix text; web.conf.spec:333 (tools.staticdir.generate_indexes = [1 | 0], default 0), web.conf.spec:308 (static_dir), web.conf.spec:303 (static_endpoint)

conditions.rationale: The directory the static file handler serves from bounds the files the application will return; the shipped value is declared, so the test is on the value rather than on the key. The spec permits an absolute path elsewhere, so the value shape is not tested.

external_dependencies: File system placement and modes of the static content directories, which decide what a reachable path can actually read, carried by the operating system.
MIME map entries added by third-party apps, carried by the app review procedure (server.conf.spec:1656).
finding_statement: Splunk Web generates directory indexes for its static content, or declares no static directory, so the application can return file types the hosted views do not need.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise ships no Web Distributed Authoring service, so there is no WebDAV module to disable; the application's share is that the remote-authoring behavior it does have - endpoints that change state through an HTTP GET - is switched off.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000085 check and fix text; web.conf.spec:198 (enable_insecure_login, default false), web.conf.spec:221 (enable_insecure_pdfgen, default false), web.conf.spec:206 (enable_secure_entity_move, default true)

conditions.rationale: The check makes enabled remote authoring a finding. This setting exposes a GET-based authentication endpoint that carries credentials in the URL; the specification defines it as a boolean with a default of false.
The specification states that when this is true the render endpoint accepts GET as well as POST, which is the authoring-through-a-URL pattern WebDAV represents; the default is false.

The specification states that when this is true the move endpoint accepts only POST, and when false it also accepts GET, which lets a view or other framework entity be relocated between apps by URL alone - a remote authoring action; the default is true.

external_dependencies: WebDAV offered by any separate web server or module placed in front of the application, carried by that component and the operating system.
finding_statement: One of Splunk Web's GET-based state-changing endpoints is enabled, so the application exposes remote authoring through a URL even though it ships no WebDAV service.

application_contribution: Splunk bounds what an app's searches and endpoints may reach: a role declares the indexes its searches are allowed to run against, and each REST endpoint declares the capability the session user must hold before it will run.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000086 check and fix text; authorize.conf.spec:292 (srchIndexesAllowed), restmap.conf.spec:111 (capability = <capabilityName>), workload_pools.conf.spec:74

conditions.rationale: The check makes access to more system resources than an application needs a finding. The specification defines this setting as the semicolon-separated list of indexes a role's searches may run against, so declaring it is how the application limits the data an app may reach.

The specification states that this setting makes the endpoint check a capability on the authenticated session user, so declaring it is how a privileged operation exposed through REST is withheld from an app that has no business invoking it.

external_dependencies: CPU, memory, and file system limits on the Splunk processes themselves, carried by the operating system through cgroups and resource limits or by the container runtime; workload_pools.conf cpu_weight and mem_weight apportion only the share already granted to the daemon and depend on host cgroup support (workload_pools.conf.spec:74, workload_pools.conf.spec:80).
Privileged operations on the host that no Splunk setting mediates, carried by the service account's own privileges and any mandatory access control policy.
finding_statement: Roles do not declare the indexes their searches may reach, or REST endpoints do not declare a required capability, so the application does not confine a hosted app's searches and endpoints to the resources it needs.

application_contribution: Splunk Web declares the endpoint prefix and the static directory its users operate within and can refuse to list those directories, and a role's search filter confines the searches run on a user's behalf to the data that role is scoped to.
citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000141-WSR-000087 check and fix text; web.conf.spec:297 (root_endpoint), web.conf.spec:308 (static_dir), web.conf.spec:333 (tools.staticdir.generate_indexes, default 0), authorize.conf.spec:150 (srchFilter)

conditions.rationale: The specification defines static_dir as the relative path the static handler serves from, which is the directory tree users are confined to for static content.
A generated directory listing lets a user walk the static tree rather than stay within the paths the views reference; the specification permits only 1 or 0 and defaults to 0.

The check extends containment to "any scripts running on the user's behalf." In Splunk, work runs on a user's behalf as a search, and srchFilter is the setting that bounds every search a role dispatches.
conditions.value: *| (empty or the override wildcard - the audit-review role must not have its reach narrowed)

conditions.rationale: root_endpoint is a [settings] key, not a stanza; it defines the URI path the appserver listens on and so bounds where content is exposed.

external_dependencies: The Splunk service account's own reach across the file system, carried by the operating system through ownership, modes, and any mandatory access control policy.
Containment of the processes themselves by chroot, namespace, or container, carried by the host.
finding_statement: Splunk Web does not declare the endpoint and static directory its users are confined to, directory listings are generated, or roles carry no search filter, so users and the searches run on their behalf are not contained to the application's own tree.

citation: Web Server SRG SRG-APP-000142-WSR-000089 check and fix text; web.conf.spec:28 (httpport, default 8000), web.conf.spec:844 (server.socket_host, 0.0.0.0 means any active interface), web.conf.spec:35 (mgmtHostPort), splunk-launch.conf.spec:79 (SPLUNK_BINDIP)

conditions.rationale: The check requires a specified port; the specification states Splunk Web will not start an HTTP listener at all if this is omitted or zero, so the port in use must be declared.

The check makes it a finding if a client can reach the server on other addresses assigned to the hosting hardware. The specification states that 0.0.0.0 means any active IPv4 interface and :: is the IPv6 equivalent, so either value leaves the listener on every address; any single address or hostname satisfies the requirement.

The specification defines this as the address and port where Splunk Web looks for the daemon and notes it otherwise listens on all available host addresses, so it must be declared for the pair to be specified rather than assumed.

Splunk Web is not the only listener on the instance; the specification defines this setting as the address the daemon's listeners bind to, so it must name an address for the management and receiving ports to be confined as well.

external_dependencies: Which address the instance is permitted to use, and any further restriction on who can reach it, carried by the host's network configuration and the firewall.
Confirming from a client that no other address answers, which the check performs by test rather than by reading configuration.
finding_statement: Splunk Web or the daemon is left listening on every interface of the host, or its port is not declared, so the application does not confine itself to one specified address and port.

application_contribution: Splunk defines distinct roles and grants each one named capabilities, so the capabilities that change the product's own configuration, its authentication, and its installed apps can be confined to administrative roles and withheld from every other role.

Which individuals hold the administrative roles, carried by the directory service and by the organization's access approval records.

Which capabilities a site-defined role may hold, which is organization-defined: the shipped role_admin holds every privileged capability by design, so the criteria name the two unprivileged roles the product ships rather than every role.
