The identity field in each audit record is written by splunkd in a fixed format with no configuration surface, so its content is confirmed by inspecting a written record.
finding_statement: The audit trail is not queued to an index (queueing = false) with no compensating input, so the account associated with each audited operation is not searchable in the repository.

application_contribution: Splunk's web access logs name the authenticated user for each request, and the audit trail names the account behind each operation. Where an authenticating proxy supplies the identity, web.conf remoteUser names the header that carries it, remoteUserMatchExact = 1 stops the dash-and-underscore header collision the specification warns of - under which "the browser could dictate the username" - and trustedIP restricts which proxy may assert it.
citation: SRG-APP-000100-WSR-000064 check text; web.conf.spec:728-748 (remoteUser = <http_header_string>, Default: REMOTE_USER, with the header-normalization caution), :767-776 (remoteUserMatchExact = [0 | 1], "Set to 1 when you set up SSO", Default: 0), :797-804 (trustedIP = <ip_addresses>, "Set to a valid IP address to enable SSO", Default: not set), :871-874 (log.access_file); restmap.conf.spec:138-142 (includeInAccessLog = <boolean>, Default: true); audit.conf.spec:23-29 ([auditTrail], queueing = <boolean>, Default: true)

conditions.rationale: The access log is the record that names the authenticated user of each Splunk Web request; an empty filename leaves no such record.
An endpoint set to false produces no splunkd_access.log entry, so the identity behind requests to it is not recorded. Default is true.
Splunk's audit records carry the acting user for operations performed through the web tier; queueing true routes them to an index. Default is true.

external_dependencies: Where single sign-on is in use, web.conf remoteUserMatchExact must be set to 1 and trustedIP must name the authenticating proxy, as the specification directs for an SSO setup. Those two settings bear on this requirement only in an SSO deployment, so they are reported here rather than tested unconditionally - a non-SSO instance legitimately leaves both at their defaults, and failing it for them would be a false finding.
The authenticating proxy or identity provider establishes the identity it asserts; the application records the identity it is given.
The user field is emitted by the product in a fixed record format with no configuration surface.
finding_statement: Splunk Enterprise has no web access log configured, excludes REST endpoints from splunkd_access.log, or has audit queueing disabled - and, where single sign-on is configured, leaves remoteUserMatchExact at 0 or trustedIP unset - so its web records do not reliably establish the identity of the user or process associated with the event.

application_contribution: Splunk's health reporter watches its own features, including the indexing and queue features that signal a log processing failure, and fires the alert actions named in health.conf when a feature holds at the threshold color; alert_actions.conf [email] configures the delivery channel. A scheduled saved search with action.email, action.email.to and an alert_condition is the product's second route to the same notification.
citation: SRG-APP-000108-WSR-000166 check text; health.conf.spec:32 ([health_reporter]), :88-91 (alert.disabled = [0|1], Default: 0), :93-94 (alert.actions = <string>), :96-99 (alert.min_duration_sec = <integer>, Default: 60), :101-103 (alert.threshold_color = [yellow|red], Default: red), :105-110 (alert.suppress_period = <integer>[m|s|h|d], Default: 10m); alert_actions.conf.spec:157-162 ([email]); savedsearches.conf.spec:73-77 (enableSched = [0 | 1], Default: 0), :270-274 (alert_condition = <search string>), :300-306 (action.email = <boolean>, Default: false; action.email.to = <email list>, REQUIRED)

conditions.rationale: The spec states that a value of 1 disables alerting for the health reporter and that "alerting for all features is disabled"; the check text requires an alert on a processing failure, so the feature must be enabled. Permitted vocabulary is [0|1] and the default is 0.
The spec defines this as the alert actions that run when an alert fires; with none named, a detected processing failure notifies nobody. The spec states no default for it.

checks.tsv marks this alert_actions.conf row key_status=stanza: the email notification stanza must exist for the health reporter's email action to have a configured delivery channel. The spec states that where an entry is not specified the default value is used.

external_dependencies: The SMTP relay that carries the notification, and the ISSO and SA addresses it is sent to, are organization-defined; alert_actions.conf holds the mail server and sender but the recipients are the organization's to supply, so the criterion tests only that the product can express them.
A processing failure that stops splunkd outright - a full filesystem, a terminated process - cannot be alerted on by the application itself and is reported by the operating system's own monitoring.
The ISSO and SA role assignments are organizational designations.
finding_statement: health.conf disables the health reporter's alerting (alert.disabled = 1), names no alert actions, or has no configured email action, so Splunk Enterprise raises no alert to the ISSO and SA when a log processing failure occurs.

application_contribution: Splunk's search layer analyzes records from every host and device together because they share one index set, and role configuration determines which of those indexes an authorized reviewer may search.
citation: OVER-REACH, and one mislabeled dependency. Removed savedsearches.conf [<stanza name>] search non_empty: the shipped savedsearches.conf declares "search =" empty, so the condition fails a stock instance, and saved searches are not required for cross-host analysis - the search layer analyzes the whole index set on demand. Separately, distsearch.conf [distributedSearch] servers was listed as an external dependency: it is Splunk configuration, which the application can reach, so that label is wrong. It is not promoted to a condition either, because an indexer-cluster search head receives its peer list from the cluster manager rather than from distsearch.conf, so a mandatory non_empty would falsely fail that topology; the assessor reads whichever of the two applies.

conditions.rationale: authorize.conf.spec: "A list of indexes that this role is allowed to search" with no default; a role whose allowed list is empty cannot review the records that the analysis must cover.

external_dependencies: Which individuals are authorized to review the analysis, and their assignment to a Splunk role, is an organizational and directory service matter.
finding_statement: No role is permitted to search the indexes holding the aggregated records (srchIndexesAllowed is unset), so cross-host analysis cannot be reviewed by the authorized individuals.

application_contribution: The Splunk search language performs on-demand filtering over the indexed records, and role configuration determines which indexes a filtering user may search.
citation: OVER-REACH, and two conditions nothing can satisfy. The original ANDed four independent features - event types, macros, saved searches and role index access - so an instance expressing its criteria through any one of them fails for lacking the other three. Two could never pass on a stock instance: the shipped eventtypes.conf and savedsearches.conf both declare "search =" empty in their default stanzas, and macros.conf is not shipped at all, so definition non_empty reads nothing. Where a site has expressed its criteria as event types, macros or saved searches, those are read as evidence of the organization-defined criteria rather than demanded as a conjunction.

conditions.rationale: authorize.conf.spec: "A list of indexes that this role is allowed to search" with no default; on-demand filtering can only reach records in the indexes a role is permitted to search.

external_dependencies: The criteria themselves - which events are of interest - are organization-defined and held in the site security plan, so the criterion tests only that the product can filter the records on demand.
On-demand filtering is performed by the search language, which is intrinsic to the product and has no configuration surface to assert.
finding_statement: No role is permitted to search the indexes holding the records (srchIndexesAllowed is unset), so on-demand filtering for events of interest cannot be performed against them.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise makes its own installed release identifiable through the product's own interfaces (the CLI version command and the server information REST endpoint), so the application supplies the release and build identifier an assessor compares against the vendor's published support policy, but it exposes no setting that sets, constrains, or attests the support status of that release.
citation: Central Log Server SRG V3R5, SRG-APP-001035-AU-000430 (V-278989), severity high, CCI-003376, SA-22 a: check text "Verify that the Central Log Server is a version supported by the vendor"; fix text "Upgrade or install a Central Log Server which is a version supported by the vendor." No product STIG rule shares CCI-003376; the sunset Splunk Enterprise 8.x for Linux STIG V2R3 states the same requirement under SPLK-CL-000510 (V-274465, CCI-002605) with fix text "Upgrade to a version supported by the vendor.", naming no configuration value. Specification basis for the absence of a setting: web.conf.spec:192-196, app.conf.spec:116-119, limits.conf.spec:3556-3559.
external_dependencies: Software deployment that fixes the installed release: the container image build or package installation pins the Splunk Enterprise release and build, and rebuilding or reinstalling is the only action that changes support status.
Splunk Enterprise software maintenance and support entitlement held for the installed release (vendor contract), which the application cannot record or enforce.
Organizational software lifecycle and patch management procedure establishing the supported-release baseline and the trigger to upgrade before vendor end of support.
The vendor's published Splunk Enterprise support policy and end-of-support dates for the installed release train, which the application does not carry and cannot evaluate.
finding_statement: This determination is made from the perspective of the application layer alone: Splunk Enterprise exposes no configuration setting that establishes or attests vendor support for its own release, so the application's share of this requirement is limited to reporting the installed release and build, and a finding is sustained only where the release the instance reports is at or past the vendor's published end of support, remedied by installing a supported release through the deployment rather than by any configuration change.
manual_reason: Support status is a property of the installed release and of the maintenance entitlement held for it, not of configuration. checks.tsv assigns no conf, stanza, or key to this requirement, and an independent sweep of all 67 Splunk 10.4.2 *.conf.spec files found no key that governs, reports, or attests vendor support or release currency: the only version-adjacent keys are web.conf.spec:192-196 (updateCheckerBaseURL, a Splunk.com release-notification URL that may be set to 0), app.conf.spec:116-119 (show_upgrade_notification, a per-app Splunk Web notice, default false), and limits.conf.spec:3556-3559 (version_upgrade_max_start_retries and the sibling version_upgrade_* keys, documented as internal KV Store migration and upgrade settings not to be changed except on vendor instruction). A phrase sweep of the same specification set for end-of-life, end-of-support, EOL, vendor support, and supported release returns zero hits. Deciding this requirement requires reading the installed package's release, which is not Splunk configuration, so no condition in the criterion vocabulary can be written over it.

application_contribution: The HTTP service in scope is the Splunk Web application server bundled inside Splunk Enterprise and started by web.conf [settings] startwebserver (web.conf.spec:23), not a separately procured and separately versioned web server product, so the application's contribution is to serve that component from the single installed Splunk Enterprise release and report that release through its own interfaces; the specification set exposes no version or support attribute for the embedded server, and no setting that makes its release a supported one.
citation: Web Server SRG V4R5, SRG-APP-001035-WSR-000340 (V-279029), severity high, CCI-003376, SA-22 a: check text "Verify that the web server is a version supported by the vendor"; fix text "Install or upgrade the webserver to a version supported by the vendor." No product STIG rule shares CCI-003376; the sunset Splunk Enterprise 8.x for Linux STIG V2R3 SPLK-CL-000510 (V-274465) fix text is "Upgrade to a version supported by the vendor.", naming no configuration value. Specification basis that the web server is an internal component of the product rather than a separately versioned one: web.conf.spec:16 [settings], web.conf.spec:23 startwebserver, web.conf.spec:28 httpport, web.conf.spec:70 enableSplunkWebSSL; only version-adjacent web setting: web.conf.spec:192-196 updateCheckerBaseURL.
external_dependencies: Software deployment that fixes the installed release: Splunk Web is patched by rebuilding or reinstalling the Splunk Enterprise package or image, and there is no separate web server package to update.
Splunk Enterprise software maintenance and support entitlement covering the installed release, which carries Splunk Web.
Organizational software lifecycle and patch management procedure establishing the supported-release baseline and the upgrade trigger before vendor end of support.

Where the organization places a separately procured HTTP front end in the boundary, that product is a distinct component assessed for version support under its own baseline and entitlement, not against the Splunk application.
finding_statement: This determination is made from the perspective of the application layer alone: the web server addressed here is the Splunk Web component of Splunk Enterprise, which exposes no configuration setting bearing on its own version support, so the application's share of this requirement is limited to serving that component from, and reporting, the single installed Splunk Enterprise release, and a finding is sustained only where that release is at or past the vendor's published end of support, or where a separately procured HTTP front end in the boundary runs an unsupported version under its own baseline, in either case remedied by upgrading the product rather than by any Splunk configuration change.
manual_reason: Splunk Web has no release or support attribute of its own: its support status is the support status of the Splunk Enterprise release that carries it, which is a property of the installed package rather than of configuration. checks.tsv assigns no conf, stanza, or key to this requirement, and the sweep of all 67 Splunk 10.4.2 *.conf.spec files returns no key reporting or constraining an embedded HTTP server version or support level; the only version-adjacent web setting is web.conf.spec:192-196 updateCheckerBaseURL, a release-notification URL that may be disabled, which does not determine support status. Deciding this requirement requires reading the installed release, which is not Splunk configuration, so no condition in the criterion vocabulary can be written over it.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise implements a report as a saved search object, so the application can carry report definitions that select audit events over a stated review range and can grant the search capability to the role that runs them on demand.
citation: savedsearches.conf.spec:31 [<stanza name>], :44 search, :564 dispatch.earliest_time, :571 dispatch.latest_time; authorize.conf.spec:67-71 [role_<roleName>] <capability> = <enabled>, :953 [capability::search]. conditions.rationale: check text "Verify the Central Log Server generates on-demand audit review and analysis reports" - a report exists in the application only where the stanza carries the search string that produces it (savedsearches.conf.spec:31, :44)

Whether reviewing personnel are available to request a report, and the incident reporting procedure the report feeds, are organizational procedures outside the application.

The closing bound of a report window, which 161 of the 182 saved searches this product ships leave unset because an open end means "to now"; a test for it reports a finding against the product as delivered.
finding_statement: Assessed at the application layer alone: Splunk Enterprise carries no saved search defining an on-demand audit review and analysis report over the audit indexes in scope, or the role that performs audit review does not hold the search capability, so the application is not configured to the fullest extent it can contribute to this requirement.

application_contribution: Splunk can define a report, dispatch it on a stated cycle, and deliver the rendered result through the email alert action, which is what carries report generation past ad hoc search into support for a reporting requirement.
citation: savedsearches.conf.spec:44 search, :73 enableSched = [0|1] default 0, :79 cron_schedule, :193 schedule_window, :300 action.email = <boolean> default false, :383 action.email.sendpdf = [1|0] default 0; alert_actions.conf.spec:157 [email].

conditions.rationale: the report that satisfies the reporting requirement exists only where the stanza carries its search string (savedsearches.conf.spec:44)

application_contribution: Splunk stamps _indextime on every event at the point its receiver accepts it and stores event time as an epoch value, which is UTC by construction. application_contribution: Splunk can run in FIPS mode, which restricts every hash, key derivation, random bit generation and signature operation in the instance to the FIPS-validated module, and its TLS version settings can be pinned so that the management, search and web channels negotiate only TLS 1.2.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise can fix the character set on both of its data-entry paths — Splunk Web decodes every string entering its controller methods as UTF-8 and forces UTF-8 on outgoing responses in place of honoring the client's Accept-Charset header, and props.conf CHARSET declares the expected encoding of data entering the indexing pipeline per source type; the fourth key attached to this requirement, override_JSON_MIME_type_with_text_plain, is charset-neutral because both permitted values emit charset=UTF-8 (web.conf.spec:364-369), so it is examined but is not a deciding operand.
citation: SRG-APP-000251-WSR-000157 check and fix text (CCI-001310, SI-10); no product STIG rule shares CCI-001310. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0): web.conf.spec:985 tools.decode.on, default true; web.conf.spec:992 tools.encode.on, default true; web.conf.spec:999 tools.encode.encoding, default utf-8, documented as overriding CherryPy's observation of the client Accept-Charset header; web.conf.spec:364 override_JSON_MIME_type_with_text_plain, both values emitting charset=UTF-8; props.conf.spec:238 CHARSET within stanza [<spec>] at props.conf.spec:80, defaults at props.conf.spec:257-259.

conditions.rationale: The check text asks whether the server limits the data set used for data entry. This is the setting that decodes all strings entering the Splunk Web controller methods as a single codec (UTF-8); the specification warns that setting it to false breaks the assumption that incoming strings are Unicode. Vendor default is true (web.conf.spec:985-990), so an unwritten key already satisfies the criterion and only an explicit disablement fails.

Fix text: configure the server to only accept the character sets expected by the hosted applications. This is the setting that encodes all controller method response strings into UTF-8; disabling it causes high byte character encoding to fail. Vendor default is true (web.conf.spec:992-997), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion.

Fix text: only accept the expected character sets. The specification states that setting this to utf-8 overwrites CherryPy's default behavior of observing the client's Accept-Charset header and forces UTF-8 output — this is precisely how the application limits rather than negotiates the character set. Permitted vocabulary is <codec>; vendor default is utf-8 (web.conf.spec:999-1007), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion and any other codec fails.

The data-entry path into the indexing pipeline is governed per source type by CHARSET, which declares the encoding Splunk assumes for input from that spec; an invalid or absent value causes further input from that spec to be discarded with a warning. Which source types carry a non-default encoding is organization-defined, so the criterion is only that a written declaration carries a value. Vendor default is UTF-8 on non-Windows and AUTO on Windows (props.conf.spec:238-259), so a source type with no declaration is already codec-fixed and is not a finding.

external_dependencies: Per-field or per-request character allow lists: the product exposes codec-level control only, so any enumeration of permitted characters is carried by the hosted Splunk apps' own input validation and their custom REST handlers.
The determination of which source types carry a non-UTF-8 encoding rests with the data owner's source inventory; the application can express the declaration but cannot decide its content.

Request-level character filtering at the perimeter is carried by the reverse proxy, load balancer or web application firewall placed in front of Splunk, assessed against that component's own baseline.
finding_statement: Splunk Enterprise does not fix the character set of its data-entry paths — web.conf [settings] tools.decode.on or tools.encode.on is set to false, tools.encode.encoding forces a codec other than UTF-8, or a props.conf CHARSET declaration is written with an empty value — so the accepted and emitted character set is negotiated from the client or left undeclared rather than limited to the set the hosted applications expect; this is assessed at the application layer alone, and per-character input validation inside the hosted apps and any perimeter filtering are recorded as external dependencies rather than as part of this finding.

application_contribution: Splunk runs its own HTTP listeners, so the product can withhold on each one the HTTP/1.1 features the Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding desync depends on (forceHttp10) and reject a request whose content length exceeds a bound (max_content_length on the splunkd REST listener, max_upload_size on Splunk Web); it exposes no setting that normalizes an ambiguous request, none that drops an unnormalizable request and closes the connection, and no HTTP/2 listener option.
citation: SRG-APP-000251-WSR-000194 check, fix and discussion text (CCI-001310, SI-10); no product STIG rule shares CCI-001310. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0): server.conf.spec:1416 forceHttp10 within stanza [httpServer] at server.conf.spec:1291, default auto; server.conf.spec:1369 max_content_length, default 2147483648 bytes, documented as rejecting HTTP requests over the configured size; web.conf.spec:1129 forceHttp10, default auto, documented as withholding HTTP/1.1 features including chunked transfer encoding when set to always; web.conf.spec:867 max_upload_size, default 500 MB; web.conf.spec:1016 tools.proxy.on and web.conf.spec:1031 tools.proxy.base.

conditions.rationale: Fix text: configure the server to interpret HTTP headers so they are normalized and unambiguous. The permitted vocabulary is auto|never|always; "never" is the value that always allows HTTP/1.1 — including persistent connections and chunked transfer encoding — even to clients the server suspects have broken HTTP/1.1 support, which is the most permissive posture toward the smuggling primitive the requirement describes. Vendor default is auto (server.conf.spec:1416-1425), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion; setting "always" withholds those features entirely and also satisfies it.

The same control for the Splunk Web listener, which is a second HTTP server in the same deployment. Permitted vocabulary auto|never|always, vendor default auto; "always" is documented as withholding HTTP/1.1 features such as persistent connections and chunked transfer encoding (web.conf.spec:1129-1140).

Fix text requires the server to validate requests that report message body length as zero in the HTTP header. max_content_length is the only application setting that rejects a request on the basis of content length — HTTP requests over the configured size are rejected. The vendor default, 2147483648 bytes, is the bound an unwritten key already enforces (server.conf.spec:1369-1378), so the application-layer criterion is that the configured bound is not raised above the product default rather than an invented number.

The equivalent message-body bound on the Splunk Web listener: the hard maximum limit, in megabytes, of uploaded files. Vendor default is 500 (web.conf.spec:867-869), so the criterion is that the bound is not raised above the product default; the units are megabytes per the specification.

external_dependencies: Normalization of an ambiguous request, and the drop-and-terminate behavior the fix text directs for requests that cannot be normalized: no Splunk setting exists for either, so this half of the objective is carried by the reverse proxy or load balancer fronting Splunk and is assessed against that component's own baseline.

The HTTP/2-only front-end to back-end path that the requirement's discussion names as the complete remedy for all smuggling variants: Splunk exposes no HTTP/2 listener setting, so it is carried by the front-end web tier.

Whether a front end is deployed at all cannot be read from Splunk configuration. Where one is, web.conf [settings] tools.proxy.on with a non-empty tools.proxy.base makes Splunk treat the front end's X-Forwarded-* headers as authoritative (web.conf.spec:1016-1032); because its correct value depends on the deployment topology rather than on the product, it is recorded here instead of being made a condition that would fail a directly exposed instance.
finding_statement: Splunk Enterprise is not configured to the fullest extent the product allows against ambiguous HTTP requests — forceHttp10 is set to never in server.conf [httpServer] or web.conf [settings], or max_content_length or max_upload_size is raised above the vendor default bound — so a listener retains the HTTP/1.1 features and the unbounded message body on which request smuggling depends; this is assessed at the application layer alone, and ambiguous-request normalization, the drop-and-close behavior and the HTTP/2 front-end path are recorded as external dependencies carried by the reverse proxy or load balancer, not as part of this finding.

application_contribution: Nothing configurable: whether the splunkd HTTP server and the Python application server tear the socket down rather than return it to the keep-alive pool when a server-level exception is raised is internal, non-configurable product behavior, so the application has no setting bearing on this requirement.
citation: SRG-APP-000251-WSR-000195 check and fix text (CCI-001310, SI-10); no product STIG rule shares CCI-001310; no conf, stanza or key is attached to this requirement in the mechanism inventory. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0), keys enumerated and excluded as non-implementing: server.conf.spec:1291 stanza [httpServer] in full; web.conf.spec:910 request.show_tracebacks; web.conf.spec:971 response.timeout; web.conf.spec:1278 appServerProcessShutdownTimeout.
external_dependencies: The bundled CherryPy-based application server and the splunkd HTTP server themselves: the teardown behavior is fixed in the product build, so any deficiency is a vendor matter recorded against the product rather than against the configuration baseline.

A behavioral test procedure — a request that forces a server-side exception against each listener in scope (management and REST port, Splunk Web, HTTP Event Collector) with the exchange captured — is required to decide the requirement, and is carried by the assessment procedure, not by configuration review.
Termination of connections on back-end exceptions where a reverse proxy or load balancer fronts Splunk, carried by that component and assessed against its own baseline.
finding_statement: No Splunk Enterprise setting governs connection termination when a server-level exception is raised, so this requirement is not decided by application configuration: any finding rests on the listener's observed teardown behavior, which is fixed in the product build, or on the front-end proxy that terminates the connection, and is recorded against those rather than against the Splunk application configuration assessed here.
manual_reason: The requirement concerns whether the HTTP server tears the connection down when an exception is raised during request handling, not whether the exception is disclosed, which is a separate requirement. Splunk Enterprise exposes no setting that conditions a connection close on a server-level exception: the whole server.conf [httpServer] stanza (server.conf.spec:1291 onward, 26 keys) carries no exception-handling or connection-termination key, and the nearest web.conf [settings] keys govern disclosure (request.show_tracebacks, web.conf.spec:910), application server shutdown (appServerProcessShutdownTimeout, web.conf.spec:1278) and response timeouts (response.timeout, web.conf.spec:971) — none of which closes a connection because an exception occurred. checks.tsv accordingly attaches no key to this requirement. Absence of a setting is not absence of the behavior, so the requirement is settled by sending a request that forces a server-side exception to each listener in scope and observing whether the response carries Connection: close and the TCP connection is torn down rather than reused; configuration cannot decide it in either direction.

application_contribution: Splunk Web can deny the enumeration the requirement is aimed at outright rather than mask it per directory: tools.staticdir.generate_indexes determines whether the web server serves a directory listing for static directories at all, and simple_error_page determines the content of the page returned when a requested page cannot be found.
citation: SRG-APP-000266-WSR-000142 check, fix and discussion text (CCI-001312, SI-11 a); no product STIG rule shares CCI-001312. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0): web.conf.spec:333 tools.staticdir.generate_indexes = [1 | 0], default 0, documented as controlling whether the webserver serves a directory listing for static directories; scoping keys web.conf.spec:297 root_endpoint, web.conf.spec:303 static_endpoint, web.conf.spec:308 static_dir; web.conf.spec:227 simple_error_page.
external_dependencies: Placing a default page in every web document directory, which the fix text directs literally: the content of the static document directory below $SPLUNK_HOME is carried by the app packaging and the installation's file layout, not by any Splunk setting.

The directories in scope are bounded by web.conf [settings] static_dir, static_endpoint and root_endpoint (web.conf.spec:308, 303, 297), which the assessor reads to scope the check; they define where the document directory is exposed and do not themselves decide the requirement.
Any directory listing served by a front-end web server, object store or CDN mapped into the same URI space is carried by that component and assessed against its own baseline.
finding_statement: web.conf [settings] tools.staticdir.generate_indexes is set to 1, so Splunk Web generates a directory listing for a static document directory instead of denying the enumeration outright; this is assessed at the application layer alone, and the placement of a default page in each web document directory is recorded as an external dependency carried by the app packaging and the installation's file layout rather than as part of this finding.
manual_reason: The only setting that decides this requirement is web.conf [settings] tools.staticdir.generate_indexes, whose documented default of 0 already denies the directory listing. Deciding it from configuration needs a criterion under which a missing key and an explicit 0 both pass, and the operator vocabulary has none: every value operator fails on a missing key, and empty fails on an explicit 0, which is the state the fix text produces. The assessor reads the value. simple_error_page does not stand in for it - the vendor default is false, and the requirement asks for a default application page rather than a minimal error page.

application_contribution: The check text looks for a mode of operation that minimizes the information returned to clients on error conditions, and Splunk Web offers exactly that choice: simple_error_page selects a page carrying only the HTTP error status in place of a verbose page, request.show_tracebacks suppresses the Python traceback that would disclose loaded module names and installation paths, and appServerProcessLogStderr keeps application server standard error — which the specification warns may carry session identifier strings — out of the Splunk log.
citation: SRG-APP-000266-WSR-000159 check and fix text (CCI-001312, SI-11 a); no product STIG rule shares CCI-001312. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0): web.conf.spec:227 simple_error_page, default false, contrasting a page containing only the error status against a verbose page containing the home link, message, results link, crashes, referrer, debug output and byline; web.conf.spec:910 request.show_tracebacks, default true, controlling whether an exception traceback is displayed to the user on fatal exceptions; web.conf.spec:1285 appServerProcessLogStderr, default false, whose text warns that appserver code may print sensitive information such as session ID strings to standard error.

conditions.rationale: This is the mode of operation the check text asks for. Set to true, Splunk Web displays a simplified error page for errors such as 404 and 500 containing only the error status; set to false it displays a more verbose page containing the home link, message, results link, crashes, referrer, debug output and byline. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is false (web.conf.spec:227-231), so the key must be written for the application's share to be met.

A Python traceback rendered to the client discloses loaded module names and paths inside the installation, which are two of the four information classes the requirement restricts. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is true (web.conf.spec:910-913), so this key must be written to false; leaving it unwritten leaves tracebacks on.

The specification states that some application server code may print sensitive information such as session ID strings to standard error, and that this setting routes that stream into splunkd.log under the UiAppServer channel; the same stream carries module and path detail from the appserver. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is false (web.conf.spec:1285-1293), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion and only an explicit enablement fails.

external_dependencies: Product identification carried in HTTP response headers and on the login page: no key in the examined specification set strips Splunk's own identification from those surfaces, so header rewriting and banner suppression are carried by the reverse proxy or load balancer fronting Splunk.
Error pages and warning text rendered by custom apps, dashboards and custom REST handlers: their templates are carried by the app developer and the app approval process, not by web.conf.

Protection of the splunkd.log content that application server standard error lands in — file permissions, retention and onward forwarding — is carried by the host operating system and the log management baseline.
finding_statement: Splunk Web is not in its information-minimizing mode — web.conf [settings] simple_error_page is not true, request.show_tracebacks is not false, or appServerProcessLogStderr is true — so error responses carry the verbose page's debug output, referrer, crash and byline detail, or a Python traceback disclosing loaded modules and installation paths; this is assessed at the application layer alone, and product identification in HTTP response headers and error templates supplied by custom apps are recorded as external dependencies rather than as part of this finding.

application_contribution: Splunk Web exposes each debugging and trace facility the requirement names as a distinct setting the product can turn off: the /debug REST endpoints (enableWebDebug), the traceback rendered to the user (request.show_tracebacks), the client-side JavaScript logger including the mode that posts to a server endpoint (js_logger_mode), dashboard performance metrics emitted to the browser console (simple_xml_perf_debug), the development auto-restart facility (engine.autoreload.on) and application server standard error reaching the Splunk log (appServerProcessLogStderr).
citation: SRG-APP-000266-WSR-000160 check and fix text (CCI-001312, SI-11 a); no product STIG rule shares CCI-001312. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0): web.conf.spec:1295 enableWebDebug, default false, controlling access to the debug REST endpoints; web.conf.spec:910 request.show_tracebacks, default true; web.conf.spec:379 js_logger_mode = [None | Firebug | Server], default None; web.conf.spec:1054 simple_xml_perf_debug, default false; web.conf.spec:915 engine.autoreload.on, default false; web.conf.spec:1285 appServerProcessLogStderr, default false.

conditions.rationale: The check text asks whether debugging information is enabled. This setting determines whether the debug REST endpoints, for example /debug/**splat, are accessible. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is false (web.conf.spec:1295-1297), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion and only an explicit enablement fails.

Fix text directs disabling debugging and trace information given to clients on error conditions; a rendered traceback is the trace information itself. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is true (web.conf.spec:910-913), so this key must be written to false for the application's share to be met.

This selects the client-side JavaScript logger mode. The permitted vocabulary is [None | Firebug | Server]: mode None logs nothing, Firebug logs through the browser debugger, and Server posts log messages to a defined server endpoint. The two non-None modes are the trace facilities the requirement names; the vendor default is None (web.conf.spec:379-388), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion.

This is a development facility: the application server auto-restarts when it detects that a Python file has changed. It belongs to the diagnostic mode of operation the requirement directs be disabled on a production instance. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is false (web.conf.spec:915-918), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion.

The specification describes this as useful when debugging issues where the appserver process fails to start, and warns that appserver code may print sensitive information such as session ID strings to standard error; enabling it is therefore the debug mode the requirement restricts. Permitted vocabulary is <boolean> and the vendor default is false (web.conf.spec:1285-1293), so an unwritten key satisfies the criterion.

external_dependencies: Debugging and developer tooling shipped inside installed Splunk apps — dashboard debug parameters, app-level logging and any diagnostic views an app provides — is carried by the app developer and the app approval process, not by web.conf.
Interpreter-level tracing, core dumps and debug symbols on the host running Splunk are carried by the operating system baseline.
Where a reverse proxy or load balancer fronts Splunk, URI filtering of the /debug path is an additional layer carried by that component and assessed against its own baseline.
finding_statement: A debugging or trace facility remains enabled in web.conf [settings] — enableWebDebug, simple_xml_perf_debug, engine.autoreload.on or appServerProcessLogStderr is true, request.show_tracebacks is not false, or js_logger_mode is set to Firebug or Server — so Splunk Web retains diagnostic output the requirement directs be disabled; this is assessed at the application layer alone, and developer tooling supplied inside installed apps and host-level tracing are recorded as external dependencies rather than as part of this finding.

application_contribution: Nothing toward installation: the application can report its installed version and build, but it has no setting that acquires, schedules or applies a security-relevant update, so the 30-day installation objective cannot be reached by configuring Splunk.
citation: SRG-APP-000456-AU-000270 check and fix text (CCI-002605, SI-2 c), severity high; attached product rule SPLK-CL-000510, whose fix text directs an upgrade to a vendor-supported version and whose check text states the STIG is sunset — no configuration setting is named. No conf, stanza or key is attached to this requirement in the mechanism inventory. Splunk 10.x specification set (Version 10.0.0), keys enumerated and excluded as non-installing: web.conf.spec:192 updateCheckerBaseURL (vendor notification only, settable to 0); app.conf.spec:116 show_upgrade_notification (app scope); serverclass.conf.spec:316 updaterRunningFilter (deployment clients with a separately installed self-updater).
external_dependencies: The organization's flaw remediation procedure for Splunk Enterprise, naming the authoritative source monitored (IAVM, CTO, DTM, STIG) and the period within which security-relevant updates are installed.
The configuration management record of upgrades performed, which is the evidence of the installation period actually met.
The vendor's currently supported release list, against which the installed version and build are compared — the basis the attached product rule SPLK-CL-000510 directs.
The package or container image build and deployment pipeline that delivers the replacement installation, assessed against its own baseline.
finding_statement: Splunk Enterprise provides no setting that installs its own updates, so this requirement is not decided by application configuration: a finding is raised only where the installed version and build are no longer on the vendor's supported release list, or where the flaw remediation record does not show security-relevant updates installed within 30 days or within the period an authoritative source directs, and it is recorded against the organization's flaw remediation process and the installed software rather than against the Splunk application configuration assessed here.
manual_reason: Splunk Enterprise does not install its own software updates. An upgrade replaces the installation from a vendor-supplied package, which is an administrative act outside the product's configuration surface, and no key in the specification set acquires, schedules or applies an update to the instance; checks.tsv accordingly attaches no conf, stanza or key to this requirement. The only update-related keys the product exposes are notification or out of scope: web.conf.spec:192 updateCheckerBaseURL merely causes Splunk Web to contact the vendor for notice of new versions and can be set to 0 to stop that contact, app.conf.spec:116 show_upgrade_notification is app scope, and serverclass.conf.spec:316 updaterRunningFilter concerns deployment clients running a separately installed self-updater rather than the Central Log Server itself. The attached product rule SPLK-CL-000510 names no setting either — its fix text directs an upgrade to a vendor-supported version and its check text states that the STIG is sunset — so the determination rests on the installed version and build, read from the running application but a property of the installed software rather than a configurable value, compared against the vendor's supported release list and against the flaw remediation record.

application_contribution: Nothing toward installation: Splunk Web can be configured to check for new vendor versions through web.conf [settings] updateCheckerBaseURL, or to stop that outbound contact by setting it to 0, but the product has no setting that acquires, schedules or applies a security-relevant update to itself.
citation: SRG-APP-000456-WSR-000187 check, fix and discussion text (CCI-002605, SI-2 c); attached product rule SPLK-CL-000510, whose fix text directs an upgrade to a vendor-supported version and whose check text states the STIG is sunset — no configuration setting is named. No conf, stanza or key is attached to this requirement in the mechanism inventory. external_dependencies: The organization's flaw remediation procedure covering the Splunk Web component of Splunk Enterprise, naming the authoritative source monitored and the installation time period.

The package or container image build and deployment pipeline that replaces the installation, assessed against its own baseline; where updateCheckerBaseURL is set to 0 for an enclave with no outbound vendor contact, the authoritative source for update notice is carried entirely by that procedure.
finding_statement: Splunk Web is not separately patchable and Splunk Enterprise provides no setting that installs its own updates, so this requirement is not decided by application configuration: a finding is raised only where the installed version and build are no longer vendor-supported, or where the flaw remediation record does not show security-relevant updates installed within 30 days or within the period an authoritative source directs, and it is recorded against the organization's flaw remediation process and the installed software rather than against the Splunk application configuration assessed here.
manual_reason: Splunk Web is a component of the Splunk Enterprise installation and is not separately patchable; it is updated when the whole installation is replaced from a vendor-supplied package. The requirement's discussion anticipates a web server configured both to check for and to install security-relevant updates, and Splunk exposes the checking half only: web.conf.spec:192 updateCheckerBaseURL causes Splunk Web to ping the vendor for notice of new versions, and setting it to 0 stops that contact, which is the value taken where outbound vendor contact is not permitted — so the key records which authoritative source the procedure must monitor rather than deciding the requirement, and it is not made a condition because neither value installs anything. No key in the specification set acquires, schedules or applies an update, and checks.tsv attaches no conf, stanza or key to this requirement. Because the objective is the installation of the update within a time period and the product provides no installation mechanism, the determination rests on the installed version and build compared against the vendor's supported release list, and on the flaw remediation and upgrade record.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise adopts the privileges of a named, non-root operating system account for splunkd (SPLUNK_OS_USER), so the account that reaches the directory tree and shell on behalf of the product is a dedicated service account rather than a privileged one; role design additionally bounds capability inheritance and delegation scope through importRoles and grantableRoles.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise requires an authenticated session on its REST endpoints and gates each custom endpoint on a named capability and, optionally, a source address list, so no anonymous write path to configuration or app content exists through the product's own interfaces.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise separates the management surface from the application surface in two ways the product itself controls: splunkd's management and REST interface listens on its own port with its own source address list and is reached by Splunk Web over the loopback address, and the capabilities that constitute management (admin_all_objects, edit_server, edit_web_settings, indexes_edit, install_apps) are withheld from the built-in non-administrative roles. Because a capability can only be granted - "enabled" is the only accepted value - withholding one is checked by its absence from a role stanza.

application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise has no setting that binds an authenticated management session to the source IP address it was established from. application_contribution: Splunk Enterprise can invalidate the tokens associated with a logged-out session, delete the session cookie when the browser quits rather than persisting it across restarts, and give authorization tokens a finite expiration so no issued identifier outlives the session indefinitely. finding_statement: Data staged for transmission leaves Splunk without the protection the product can apply: the [tcpout:<group>] output lacks a client certificate, does not pin sslVersions to tls1.2, does not verify the receiver's certificate or does not use indexer acknowledgment, or the email alert action does not verify the SMTP server's certificate on an approved TLS version.

citation: SRG-APP-000442-WSR-000182 check text; SPLK-CL-000460 fix text; SPLK-CL-000330 fix text; SPLK-CL-000430 fix text; inputs.conf.spec:922-937, 986-1060, 1665-1670, 1801-1815; server.conf.spec:724-734, 858-877; web.conf.spec:70-73, 151-160

conditions.rationale: inputs.conf.spec:1665-1670 makes this the TLS switch for the HTTP Event Collector, so clearing it means events are received in clear text.

The SPLK-CL-000460 fix text sets serverCert on the receiving port; the setting is declared for this stanza at inputs.conf.spec:926 and described at inputs.conf.spec:990-1000, and without it the receiver cannot complete a TLS handshake.
The SPLK-CL-000430 fix text gives sslVersions = tls1.2 for inputs.conf; inputs.conf.spec:929 and 1035-1047 define the value for incoming connections.

inputs.conf.spec:930 and 1052-1060 state that an unset value uses the OpenSSL default string; the regex accepts only the explicit AES with SHA-2 list form of the SPLK-CL-000430 cipherSuite value, which is what keeps reception off weak cryptography.
server.conf.spec:724-734 makes this the switch for TLS on the management and KV Store ports, which receive REST, deployment client and distributed search traffic.
web.conf.spec:70-73 gives a default of false and SPLK-CL-000330 requires the value 1, so without it Splunk Web receives credentials and search input over plain HTTP.

external_dependencies: Sending clients, forwarders and browsers, which must themselves use TLS on the approved version
Certificate authority and key material placed on the host per SPLK-CL-000450
Host operating system firewall, which decides whether any non-TLS receiver port is reachable at all
FIPS validated cryptographic module supplied by the host operating system

Organizational decision to require mutual authentication, which inputs.conf requireClientCert, server.conf [sslConfig] requireClientCert and web.conf requireClientCert express but which neither the check text nor the product STIG mandates
finding_statement: A Splunk receiving port accepts data without the protection the product can apply: inputs.conf [http] enableSSL, server.conf enableSplunkdSSL or web.conf enableSplunkWebSSL is disabled, or the [splunktcp-ssl:<port>] receiver has no certificate, is not pinned to tls1.2, or permits a cipher outside the approved AES with SHA-2 list.

application_contribution: Splunk can be placed in FIPS mode through splunk-launch.conf so that its digital signature, hashing and TLS functions use only FIPS-validated algorithms, which is the single switch the product exposes for this requirement.
citation: SRG-APP-000514-AU-002890 check text; SPLK-CL-000390 check and fix text; splunk-launch.conf.spec:110-127

conditions.rationale: The SPLK-CL-000390 fix text sets SPLUNK_FIPS=1 in splunk-launch.conf before the first start, and its check text expects "splunk show fips-mode" to report FIPS mode enabled; the permitted vocabulary is [0|1] at splunk-launch.conf.spec:110-127, which also records that the setting is one time only and that a later change requires a reinstall.

external_dependencies: The FIPS 140 validated cryptographic module supplied by the host operating system, which Splunk calls into and which splunk-launch.conf.spec:114-116 notes can itself place the instance in FIPS mode when the kernel runs in FIPS mode
The installation procedure, because the SPLK-CL-000390 fix text states FIPS mode must be set before the initial start and otherwise requires a reinstall or upgrade
SPLUNK_COMMON_CRITERIA=1, which the SPLK-CL-000390 fix text sets alongside SPLUNK_FIPS but which this release's splunk-launch.conf specification does not document
finding_statement: splunk-launch.conf does not set SPLUNK_FIPS = 1, so the instance does not run in FIPS mode and its digital signature, hashing and confidentiality functions are not restricted to FIPS-validated algorithms.

application_contribution: Splunk can be pointed at a single organization-curated PEM trust store, restricted to that store rather than the operating system's anchors, made to validate the certificates it is presented, and made to check certificate revocation status.
citation: SRG-APP-000910-AU-000390 check text; SPLK-CL-000450 check and fix text; server.conf.spec:798-824, 902-937, 996-1009, 1125-1145, 5392; outputs.conf.spec:691-699

conditions.rationale: The SPLK-CL-000450 fix text requires the DOD root CA public certificate to be placed for Splunk use; server.conf.spec:996-1009 defines this as the single concatenated PEM certificate authority store and states a value is required when the instance runs in Common Criteria mode.

server.conf.spec:902-920 gives the vocabulary splunk and OS (values are not case sensitive): splunk uses only the certificate authority certificates in the sslRootCAPath store, while OS admits the operating system's anchors, which are not the store the organization curates for this application; caTrustStorePath applies only when the value is OS (server.conf.spec:922-937).

server.conf.spec:1125-1145 states that crl is the only accepted value and that the default empty string turns certificate status validation off, so without it a revoked certificate issued under a trusted anchor is still accepted; the revocation files themselves live under $SPLUNK_HOME/auth/crl at the path given by [kvstore] sslCRLPath (server.conf.spec:5392), not in [sslConfig] as the check inventory records, so no condition is written over sslCRLPath.
server.conf.spec:798-824 gives a default of false, meaning any valid-looking certificate is accepted; a trust store only has effect once presented certificates are actually validated against it.

outputs.conf.spec:691-699 deprecates this setting in favor of server.conf [sslConfig] sslRootCAPath and states it is used only when that setting is unset, so leaving it unset keeps one organization-managed trust store rather than a second per-output set of anchors.

external_dependencies: The content of the trust store file, which the organization populates with approved anchors and which the SPLK-CL-000450 check text verifies with openssl on the host operating system
Operating system file permissions on the trust store and certificate revocation list files
The certificate authority's revocation list distribution, which must be retrieved and placed on the host for crl validation to have data
The organization's determination of which trust anchors are approved
finding_statement: Splunk does not restrict certificate validation to the organization-managed trust store: server.conf [sslConfig] sslRootCAPath is unset, caTrustStore admits the operating system anchors, certificate status validation is off, server certificates are not verified, or a deprecated per-output trust store is still configured in outputs.conf.

application_contribution: Splunk Web validates certificates through the same splunkd trust store, so the application's contribution is a single organization-curated PEM store, the restriction of validation to that store, and revocation checking.
citation: SRG-APP-000910-WSR-000300 check text; SPLK-CL-000450 check and fix text; server.conf.spec:902-937, 996-1009, 1125-1145; web.conf.spec:108-130

conditions.rationale: web.conf.spec:108-118 states that Splunk Web falls back to the server.conf [sslConfig] sslRootCAPath value and never overrides it, so that file is the trust store for the web interface; server.conf.spec:996-1009 defines it as the concatenated PEM certificate authority store and the SPLK-CL-000450 fix text requires the approved root CA certificate to be placed for Splunk use.

server.conf.spec:902-920 gives the vocabulary splunk and OS: splunk uses only the anchors in the sslRootCAPath store, while OS admits the operating system's anchors, which the organization does not curate for this application.

server.conf.spec:1125-1145 states that crl is the only accepted value, that the default empty string turns status validation off, and that when active it applies to Splunk Web as well as splunkd and Splunk-to-Splunk channels.

external_dependencies: The content of the trust store file, which the organization populates with approved anchors and which the SPLK-CL-000450 check text verifies with openssl on the host operating system
Operating system file permissions on the trust store and revocation list files
web.conf sslRootCAPath and requireClientCert, which take effect only for certificate based user authentication (web.conf.spec:108-130) and so cannot carry this requirement on their own
Any TLS terminating reverse proxy in front of Splunk Web, which holds its own trust store
finding_statement: Splunk Web does not restrict certificate validation to the organization-managed trust store: server.conf [sslConfig] sslRootCAPath is unset, caTrustStore admits the operating system anchors, or certificate status validation is off.

application_contribution: Splunk can hold its private keys in password-protected PEM files named from configuration and stores those passwords in its own encrypted form rather than in clear text, which is the key protection the product itself can express.
citation: SRG-APP-000915-AU-000400 check text; SPLK-CL-000450 fix text; inputs.conf.spec:990-1006; server.conf.spec:971-1009

conditions.rationale: inputs.conf.spec:990-1000 states that the daemon auto-generates certificates on first start and that these must be replaced where applicable with an organization-issued PEM certificate, so naming the certificate is what puts the key under organizational control.

inputs.conf.spec:1002-1006 states the password is entered in plain text once and that the input then encrypts and rewrites it to inputs.conf, so a stored value that does not begin with Splunk's encrypted marker is still a clear-text key password.

server.conf.spec:971-983 shows this path as the certificate the daemon auto-generates on first start and directs that it be replaced with one created or obtained by the organization; the SPLK-CL-000450 fix text requires an approved certificate.

server.conf.spec:989-991 gives the vendor default of "password" for the auto-generated certificate, so a value that is not in Splunk's encrypted form leaves the private key protected by a published default or by nothing.

server.conf.spec:996-1009 states a value is required when the instance runs in Common Criteria mode and defines the store the instance validates against, so the key material it holds is under the same organizational control as the server key.

external_dependencies: Organization-defined safeguards for key storage, such as file system permissions, disk encryption or a hardware protected key store, which the check text leaves to the organization
Any hardware security module or external key store, which this release's configuration files do not reference
The splunk.secret file and its operating system permissions, which protect the encryption of the stored passwords
Operating system ownership and permission bits on the certificate and private key files
finding_statement: Splunk's private key material is not protected to the extent the product allows: a certificate password is stored in clear text or left at the vendor default, or the instance still presents the certificate and key it auto-generated on first start.

application_contribution: Splunk Web can name an organization-issued certificate and private key in place of the auto-generated pair and can hold a password on that private key, which is the key protection the web interface's configuration can express.
citation: SRG-APP-000915-WSR-000310 check text; SPLK-CL-000330 fix text; web.conf.spec:75-98

conditions.rationale: web.conf.spec:75-81 shows this path as the auto-generated default private key, and the SPLK-CL-000330 fix text requires the private key generated for the approved certificate, so the default value means the shipped key is still in use.
web.conf.spec:82-92 shows this path as the auto-generated default certificate; SPLK-CL-000330 requires the approved certificate in PEM format.

web.conf.spec:93-98 states that this password protects the private key named by privKeyPath and that the default is the unencrypted private key, so a value present is the safeguard the product expresses; the same lines record that an encrypted key cannot be combined with splunkd client authentication, which is an organization-defined trade-off rather than a product limit.

external_dependencies: Organization-defined safeguards for key storage, such as file system permissions, disk encryption or a hardware protected key store, which the check text leaves to the organization
Any hardware security module or external key store, which web.conf does not reference
Operating system ownership and permission bits on the Splunk Web certificate and key files
The splunk.secret file and its permissions, which protect the stored password's encryption
finding_statement: Splunk Web's private key is not protected to the extent the product allows: privKeyPath and serverCert still name the auto-generated default files, or sslPassword is unset so the private key is stored without a password.

application_contribution: Splunk has no NTP client, so its share is to bound and act on clock divergence between its own components, refusing to register a search peer beyond addpeer_skew_limit and warning beyond max_tolerable_skew, and to remove time zone ambiguity from event timestamps with props.conf TZ and TZ_ALIAS.
citation: SRG-APP-000920-AU-000410 check text; SRG-APP-000086-AU-000030 check text; limits.conf.spec:493-502, 529-536; props.conf.spec:580-612

conditions.rationale: limits.conf.spec:493-502 states that a search peer is not added when the skew between search head and peer exceeds this value in seconds; the tolerance is an organization-defined number, so the application's testable share is that the product expresses the bound (default 600).

limits.conf.spec:529-536 states that a warning is logged when the skew between the search head clock and a peer clock exceeds this value in seconds; the tolerance is organization-defined, so presence is the application's share (default 60).

external_dependencies: The host operating system's time service (NTP or chrony), which is where the Central Log Server SRG itself places time synchronization when the log server application has no NTP client (SRG-APP-000086-AU-000030 check text)
The authoritative time source shared with the host and with the devices in scope of coverage

Forwarder and sending device clocks, which set the event timestamps Splunk records; props.conf TZ is left unset where the time zone of the host running splunkd or the forwarder-supplied zone is the intended source (props.conf.spec:580-590)
Operating system and network device STIGs, which carry the synchronization requirement for those components
finding_statement: Splunk expresses no clock skew bound between its own components (limits.conf [search] addpeer_skew_limit or max_tolerable_skew is not available in the assessed configuration), so divergence between the search head and its peers is neither refused nor reported.

application_contribution: Splunk Web has no NTP client and takes its clock from the host, so the application's share is the skew bound it enforces between the search head and its peers and the unambiguous time zone it applies to events and to the user interface.
citation: SRG-APP-000920-WSR-000320 check text; SRG-APP-000086-AU-000030 check text; limits.conf.spec:493-502, 529-536; props.conf.spec:580-590; user-prefs.conf.spec:53-58

conditions.rationale: limits.conf.spec:493-502 states that a search peer whose clock differs from the search head by more than this value in seconds is not added; the number is an organization-defined tolerance, so presence is the application's testable share.
limits.conf.spec:529-536 states that exceeding this skew between the search head and a peer logs a warning, which is how the application reports divergence it cannot correct.

external_dependencies: The host operating system's time service (NTP or chrony), which synchronizes the clock Splunk Web reads
The authoritative time source shared with the host and with the devices in scope of coverage

props.conf TZ, which is set per source type in a [<spec>] stanza and is correctly left unset where the host or forwarder time zone is intended (props.conf.spec:580-590), and user-prefs.conf [general] tz, which is a per-user display preference that falls back to the search head time zone when unset (user-prefs.conf.spec:53-58)
Operating system STIG settings for the time service
finding_statement: Splunk expresses no clock skew bound between its own components (limits.conf [search] addpeer_skew_limit or max_tolerable_skew is not available in the assessed configuration), so divergence between the search head serving the web interface and its peers is neither refused nor reported.

application_contribution: Splunk compares its own clock against each search peer's clock when the peer is registered and on distributed searches, and expresses the tolerated difference through addpeer_skew_limit and max_tolerable_skew; the comparison frequency and the authoritative source are not application settings.
citation: SRG-APP-000925-AU-000420 check text; limits.conf.spec:180, 493-502, 529-536, 3676

conditions.rationale: limits.conf.spec:493-502 defines the largest tolerated difference in seconds when a search peer is configured from a search head, which is the comparison the application performs; the value is organization-defined, so presence is its testable share.

limits.conf.spec:529-536 defines the largest tolerated difference in seconds between the search head and peer clocks, above which a warning is logged; limits.conf interval is not a setting of the [search] stanza in this release (limits.conf.spec:180 is [default] and 3676 is [metrics]), so no condition is written over it.

external_dependencies: The host operating system's time service, which performs the comparison against the authoritative time source and corrects the clock
The organization-defined comparison frequency and the identity of the authoritative time source, which are policy determinations the application cannot hold
Operating system STIG settings for the time service, such as the chrony or ntpd polling interval
finding_statement: Splunk expresses no tolerated difference for the clock comparison it performs against its search peers (limits.conf [search] max_tolerable_skew or addpeer_skew_limit is not available in the assessed configuration), so a divergent peer clock is neither reported nor refused.

application_contribution: The search head behind Splunk Web compares its clock against each peer's clock at peer registration and during distributed search, and the tolerated difference is the one value the application expresses; the frequency and the authoritative source are not application settings.
citation: SRG-APP-000925-WSR-000330 check text; limits.conf.spec:493-502, 529-536

conditions.rationale: limits.conf.spec:493-502 defines the largest tolerated clock difference in seconds at peer registration, which is the internal comparison the product performs; the number is organization-defined.
limits.conf.spec:529-536 defines the largest tolerated running clock difference in seconds between the search head and a peer, above which the product logs a warning.

external_dependencies: The host operating system's time service, which compares the internal clock with the authoritative time source on its own schedule
The organization-defined comparison frequency and the identity of the authoritative time source
Operating system STIG settings for the time service polling interval
finding_statement: Splunk expresses no tolerated difference for the clock comparison the search head performs against its peers (limits.conf [search] max_tolerable_skew or addpeer_skew_limit is not available in the assessed configuration), so a divergent clock behind the web interface is neither reported nor refused.
